---
title: "1. Factorisation"
engine: pari-gp
format: html
---

Factorisation is what PARI/GP is known for, and it is a good first thing to
try, because the answers are big enough to be inconvenient anywhere else.

## Integers

```{gp}
factor(2^128 + 1)
```

That is the seventh Fermat number, and gp is not impressed by it. The
factorisation comes back as a matrix of primes and exponents, so it can be
used as data rather than read as text:

```{gp}
f = factor(2^128 + 1);
[matsize(f), f[1, 1], f[2, 1]]
```

`factorint` takes a flag saying how hard to try, which matters when a number
has a large second-largest factor:

```{gp}
factorint(10^40 + 1, 1)
```

## Divisors and multiplicative functions

The factorisation is what every multiplicative function is computed from:

```{gp}
divisors(360)
```

```{gp}
[sigma(360), eulerphi(360), moebius(30), omega(360), bigomega(360)]
```

## Polynomials

The same word means several things, and gp wants to know which:

```{gp}
factor(x^6 - 1)
```

Over a finite field:

```{gp}
factormod(x^4 + 1, 5)
```

Over the 5-adics, to four digits of precision:

```{gp}
factorpadic(x^2 + 1, 5, 4)
```

And over a number field — here $\mathbb{Q}(i)$, where $x^2+1$ finally splits:

```{gp}
nffactor(nfinit(y^2 + 1), x^2 + 1)
```
